result:
**I would pick PostgreSQL, with a JSONB column for the variable attributes.** It gives you most of MongoDB's schema flexibility while keeping relational guarantees for the parts of a catalogue that are relational.

| Concern | PostgreSQL (+ JSONB) | MongoDB |
|---|---|---|
| Varied attributes per product | JSONB column, with no migration to add an attribute | Native document model, slightly more natural |
| Querying attributes | A GIN index covers containment queries on arbitrary keys; range queries need expression indexes per attribute | Rich query operators; wildcard indexes cover arbitrary keys |
| Relational data (categories, brands, variants, pricing, inventory) | Foreign keys, joins and constraints built in | `$lookup` works but is clumsier, and integrity is enforced in application code |
| Transactions | Mature, cheap, across any tables | Multi-document transactions exist but cost more and have more caveats |
| Schema enforcement | Strict columns for the core fields; JSONB validation is weaker (CHECK constraints or an extension) | Built-in optional JSON Schema validators |
| Faceted search and aggregation | Possible in SQL, awkward over JSONB at scale | Aggregation pipeline is good at this |
| Horizontal write scaling | Single primary plus read replicas; sharding needs Citus or similar | Built-in sharding |
| Reporting | SQL, with joins to orders and stock | Usually needs an export or a connector |

**Why PostgreSQL:**
- **A catalogue is only partly schemaless.** SKU, name, price, category, brand and stock are fixed and relational, and only the long tail of attributes varies. Typed columns for the core plus JSONB for the tail fits that shape.
- **Products get joined to everything.** Orders, inventory, pricing rules and promotions all reference them, and you will want foreign keys and transactions there.
- **Scale is rarely the constraint.** Catalogues are read-heavy and usually millions of rows, not billions, so a single node with replicas has a lot of headroom.

**The PostgreSQL costs to accept:**
- **JSONB statistics are poor.** The planner can misestimate attribute filters, so promote hot attributes to real or generated columns.
- **Updates rewrite the whole JSONB value.** Keep the attribute blobs modest in size.
- **Attribute validation is your job.** A common approach is an `attribute_definitions` table per category, checked in the application.

**When I would pick MongoDB instead:**
- The catalogue is a standalone service with little relational data around it.
- Products are deeply nested, heterogeneous documents that are read and written whole.
- You expect write volume or data size that needs sharding from the start.
- The team already runs MongoDB well and has no PostgreSQL experience.

Either way, if you need serious faceted search (typo tolerance, relevance ranking, facet counts across many attributes), plan on a search engine such as OpenSearch or Typesense alongside the database.
